reason: Start with Hobbes’s account of authorization to examine the basis and limits of obedience.
expectation: I expect an account of how a sovereign gains authority, though the limit of obedience may require another step.

alternatives.reason: Locke’s consent and majority rule also address authority, but I’ll start with Hobbes.

effect: Hobbes’s authorization is linked to securing peace, so I’ll test its limit when protection fails.
reaction: The qualification that concentrated power may fail makes the claim more interesting.
reason: Combine the sovereign’s purpose with failed protection to address Hobbes’s limit on obedience.
expectation: I expect Hobbes to allow a subject some freedom to resist or withdraw obedience when the sovereign cannot protect them.

alternatives.reason: I also considered starting Locke’s account, but finishing the Hobbes question first seems efficient.

effect: Hobbes’s duty of obedience can end when protection is lost, not merely when a subject dislikes a decision. I’ll move to Locke’s account.
reaction: The distinction makes the limit more concrete.
reason: This is the only available combination and begins the remaining Locke goal.

effect: Locke’s account links consent and majority decisions to a trust to protect lives, liberty and possessions; I’ll test what happens when rulers violate it.
reaction: The distinction between consent and permission for arbitrary seizure is useful.
reason: This is the only available combination and directly addresses the remaining goal about breach of trust.
expectation: I expect arbitrary seizure to count as a breach of political trust that can justify resistance, though the exact conditions may matter.

effect: Locke treats seizure for private use as a breach of trust that can justify resistance, distinct from Hobbes’s limit based on lost protection.
reaction: The concrete harvest example made the contrast clear, though resistance is not guaranteed to succeed.

mostWorthwhile.text: Testing Locke’s account against arbitrary seizure was most worthwhile: it connected consent and political trust to a concrete case.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial authorization step was the least engaging; it established Hobbes’s premise but was brief and predictable.

surprise.text: Hobbes’s account also allows obedience to end when protection is lost, though that differs from Locke’s breach-of-trust argument.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the last two combinations were the only available gameplay choices.

continue.text: Yes. I would continue to see more concrete comparisons between political theories; the distinction between protection and trust was useful.
